marie (runtime): Hey folks — running long nsys traces to debug KV cache kernel selection. Files blow up to 15–30GB and I get drowned in kernels. Any tips for CLI flags to limit size but keep useful kernel timelines?

alex (perf): If you only need kernel timelines around K/V hits, use NVTX ranges to bound capture. start your test, mark nvtx ranges around the hot path, then run: 

```
nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt --output=/tmp/kv_short --capture-range=nvtx --duration=12s
```

That keeps the capture focused and much smaller.

praveen: Also try disabling sampling if you only want full kernel timelines: `--sample=none` (nsys default is often sampling for OSRT/timers). For long traces you can do a rolling capture: short 10s windows triggered by an NVTX event then concat. That avoids single huge qdrep files.

sara: Two more practical things we do: 1) drop `nvtx` if you don't need user ranges — that reduces overhead. 2) use `--output` to write to an SSD or tmpfs so it doesn't stall the system. And compress after: `nsys export -f sqlite --output trace.sqlite trace.qdrep` then gzip the sqlite.

marie (runtime): Good call on tmpfs — I was writing to NFS. For batching heuristics I still need per-kernel timing resolution (osrt). Is it safe to keep `osrt` enabled with `--sample=none`?

alex (perf): Yes, `--trace=osrt` gives the high-resolution OS timers for CUDA kernels and can be used with sample=none. But be mindful: osrt + full cuda timeline = big files. If you're profiling many concurrent streams, prefer short windows and NVTX delimiters.

praveen: If you want to profile only one process on a multi-tenant box, use `--pid` or capture-range options (e.g., `--capture-range=pid:12345`) so nsys ignores other noise. Combine with `--duration` so it auto-stops.

ops-bot: Reminder: scheduled nsys captures on gpu-node-12 from 12:10 to 12:30 — job id 7843. :robot_face:

sara: Another trick — use NVTX counters to log token counts/seq len into ranges, then post-filter the qdrep by those ranges to map long kernels to decoding position. Makes batching heuristics easier to reason about.

marie (runtime): Awesome — last q: are there recommended sample intervals if I do sampling instead of full tracing? I want to catch sporadic long kernels but not full detail.

alex (perf): For sporadic hotspots, sampling with a 5–20ms interval is a sweet spot for latency anomalies. Example:

```
nsys profile --trace=cuda,osrt --sample=timer --sample-interval=10ms --output=/tmp/kv_sample
```
You lose per-call timeline but get aggregated hotspots and much smaller files.

praveen: And run `nsys stats` or the UI to generate summaries — often that's enough to point to the offending kernel and you can then run a focused NVTX-bounded capture.

marie (runtime): Perfect. I'll switch to tmpfs + nvtx-bounded short captures and fall back to sampling for broader sweeps. Thanks! :rocket:

alex (perf): ping me if you want me to review a trace; I can usually spot kernel misselection patterns quickly.

sara: saved some of our standard commands to the eng-runtime wiki under 'nsys playbook' — will paste a link later.

marie (runtime): Nice. If anyone has an example nvtx instrumentation snippet for our runtime (C++/CUDA) share here pls.
